analysis.one_liner: Blocks the consumer bureau from regulating payday and car-title loans for two years and lets states opt out.
analysis.headline: With a single cosponsor, the bill never left the House Financial Services Committee — no hearing, no vote — and the consumer bureau's authority over payday loans stayed intact.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Mick Mulvaney's bill would have stopped the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from issuing or enforcing any rules on payday, car-title, and similar loans for 24 months. After that, the bureau could issue a rule only after consulting state, tribal, and local officials, completing studies, and publishing a report — and any state or federally recognized tribe could get a five-year waiver from the rule, renewable indefinitely. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Payday and car-title lenders. They would have received a two-year break from any federal rules covering their products, and afterward a permanent escape hatch: any state or tribe could waive the federal rule for five years at a time, forever. The required studies, consultations, and public reports would have added more delay before any rule took effect.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the CFPB from issuing or enforcing any rule on payday loans, vehicle title loans, or similar loans for 24 months after enactment — a freeze that would have covered the rulemaking the bureau had begun in 2015.

Requires the bureau to consult with officials in every affected jurisdiction, conduct studies of its own authority and the rule's effects, and publish a public report before any payday loan rule could be finalized.
Obliges the bureau to grant any state or federally recognized tribe a five-year waiver from any final payday loan rule, renewable every five years — letting each jurisdiction opt out indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: People who take out payday and car-title loans, most of them low-income households facing a cash shortfall. Fees, interest rates, and repeat borrowing would stay federally unregulated during the moratorium, and in states or tribal areas that waived the rules, no federal protections would apply at all.

drawbacks.text: For the people the bill claimed to serve — residents of states and tribal lands — the practical effect was fewer protections: a 24-month freeze on federal rules, followed by a rule that any state or tribe could waive, meaning borrowers in waiving jurisdictions would have no federal limits on fees and rollovers.
The waiver provision goes beyond deferring to state rules: it lets states nullify a federal consumer protection entirely, so a 'federal floor' would only apply where states chose to accept it.

The bill's strongest good-faith argument was federalism: states, tribes, and cities already regulate these loans in varied ways, and a single federal standard could displace tailored local approaches. The bill's findings argue states are capable of protecting their own citizens without a federal floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary borrowers, the costs outweighed the benefits. The federalism framing in the bill's findings sits awkwardly next to its actual mechanism: it would not have strengthened state authority, but handed every state and tribe a standing veto over a federal consumer rule, on top of a two-year moratorium timed to the bureau's first-ever payday rulemaking. The main beneficiaries would have been the lenders themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mick Mulvaney introduced the bill on March 14, 2016, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, drawing one Republican cosponsor and no other support.

The bill responded directly to rulemaking the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau had set in motion — it cites the bureau's March 26, 2015 outline of proposals for payday, vehicle title, and similar loans, and the bureau's stated aim of establishing a federal consumer protection floor.
The committee never reported the bill or scheduled any action, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers of small-dollar loans are better off than they would have been under the bill, and the CFPB kept its authority to regulate payday loans without a moratorium or state waivers. Payday lenders, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Mick Mulvaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would have imposed a 24-month moratorium on CFPB payday rules and let states and tribes waive any final rule indefinitely.

for.name: Payday and auto-title lending industry
for.what_they_did: Would have been shielded from the CFPB's payday rule by the moratorium and waiver structure; widely reported as a source of Mulvaney's campaign support and as backing similar efforts to block the bureau's payday rulemaking.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
against.role: Federal regulator whose payday rulemaking the bill would have blocked
against.what_they_did: Had released an outline of proposed payday, vehicle title, and similar loan rules in March 2015, which the bill would have prohibited from taking effect for two years and subjected to waivers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only recorded support came from two Republicans — sponsor Mulvaney and one Republican cosponsor; no Democrats signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would have frozen any federal rule for two years and then let any state or tribe waive it in renewable five-year blocks, protecting lenders' high-fee, short-term business model. Their gain comes directly at borrowers' expense, since the loans' cost structure depends on fees and repeat borrowing.

The waiver provision would have exempted tribal trust lands from any federal payday rule at a tribe's request, a shelter for lenders operating under tribal law. Borrowers on those lands would have lost the federal protections the rule offered.

The bill would have stripped the bureau of authority over this loan market for two years and conditioned any future rule on studies, reports, and state-by-state waivers. Its interest in regulating the market ran alongside borrowers' interest in protections.
